content.thinking:
I'm planning out a whimsical biplane design with a chubby fuselage, round nose cowl, big wheels, and cheerful cream, red, teal, and yellow coloring, sized roughly 8m wingspan by 6.5m length, including a pilot with goggles and scarf before working out the actual coordinates.

Now I'm working through the skeleton joints for the propeller, rudder, ailerons, and wheels, then building the wing geometry as extruded rounded polygon outlines...

Placing decals on the wing top and underside with slight offsets, then shrinking the lower wing's span. Now I'm sketching the fuselage as a loft along the z-axis with tapering width/height stations from a plump mid-body down to a slender tail and nose.

I'm layering the paint scheme: a red cel base countershaded with a cream belly, plus a cream band decal across a mid-body section. For the nose, I'm switching to a lathed cowl shape defined by a radius/height profile along the z-axis.

Now I'm building the propeller assembly — a spinner cone at the tip, a hinge joint for the prop, and two blades extruded from a tapered leaf-shaped outline with slight thickness.

For materials I'm painting the blades wood-colored with yellow tips based on distance from the hub, and planning a dark recessed cockpit cutout sitting on top of the fuselage near the nose.

Now I'm designing the pilot: a torso and head as separate joints, with goggles made from dark lens cylinders and a strap torus, plus a brown leather cap shaped from a partial sphere, and considering a trailing scarf sweep for flair.

For the face I'll keep it simple with a small pink nose, skip the mouth, and add a whimsical mustache from two scaled spheres, with the goggles' white lens discs showing pupils underneath. The windshield gets a thin light-blue frame rather than a full glass pane.

Now I'm working out the strut placement connecting the wings and fuselage—lower wing meeting the fuselage near its base, upper wing positioned above and forward of the cockpit, with the pilot's head tucked just behind the upper wing's chord.

I'm repositioning the upper wing further forward and shifting the pilot's head back slightly so it clears the wing above it, then plotting out the cabane struts connecting fuselage to upper wing and the interplane struts linking lower and upper wings at staggered front/back x-positions, using thin cream-colored rods for a streamlined look.

I'm adding thin dark bracing wires crossing diagonally between the strut bases and tops, then working out joint placement and box geometry for the ailerons on the trailing edges of both wings, positioning their hinge joints to aim outward along the wingspan.

Now I'm defining the tail assembly: a stabilizer extruded near the rear of the fuselage, an elevator hinged behind it, and a rudder fin extruded in the y-z plane facing forward.

Still defining fin and rudder outlines...

I'm extending the fuselage tail loft slightly further back and computing the extrusion axis for the fin so the thickness points along the correct direction. Now I'm planning simple geometry for the tail skid and landing gear struts.

Still writing landing gear struts...

Checking proportions: wheel bottom clears the floor with the axle set at 0.46, and overall plane height comes to about 2.55m against a real Stearman's 3m, which feels reasonable. For added realism I'm planning exhaust pipes on the cowl sides, dark cooling vent slots, a rivet ring of merged spheres around the cowl, and subtle panel line details on the fuselage.

Now I'm thinking through decals—painting stripes, a "7" number, and "BARNEY" text on the tail and fuselage using surface decals oriented outward so they read correctly without mirroring, placed near the fuselage surface accounting for its width tapering at the tail. I also want to add wing roundels using circular decal graphics with rings and a star.

I'm figuring out the color palette for the plane, limited to around 64 flat colors, with reds, creams, teals, yellows, and browns for the leather accents, plus planning the wing paint scheme with a cream base and red tip accents.

For the wing coloring logic, red fills the outer tip sections while the top surface gets subtle rib lines using a modulo pattern on the x-position to create thin darker stripes spaced across the wing.

I'm defining the cel-shaded paint constants once so they can be reused, each carrying both a lit and shadow color variant. For the leading edge accent, I'm using the outline y-coordinate to detect the front edge of the wing and paint it red when it exceeds a threshold.

Now I'm shifting to the exhaust pipes, building curved sweep paths along the cowl using Catmull-Rom points that taper from front to rear with a dark metal finish. For the cowl itself, I'm setting up a lathe shape with an axis-aligned outline that bulges out to the fuselage radius before tapering back to the axis.

For coloring, I'm applying a cel-shaded paint rule based on the lathe's radial height: yellow near the widest band, cream closest to the axis, and teal elsewhere, giving the cowl a painted-ring look. I'm also positioning the propeller hub and spinner cone just ahead of the cowl's front face.

Now I'm sizing the fuselage loft station so it sits properly inside the cowl's radius, and planning a ring of eight small dark vent boxes around the cowl front using a ring-frame generator -- working out how the ring items' outward-facing axis aligns with the line direction so the vents seat correctly against the cowl surface.

I'm also adding a ring of twenty small brass rivet spheres embedded into the cowl wall at the correct radius matching the fuselage outline at that height, and checking that the frame-generated items properly inherit a nearest bone/joint for skinning since the literal frame itself carries no bone reference.

Rather than let the rivets risk attaching to the nearby prop joint and spinning with the propeller, I'll explicitly pass a `bone: body` option to every part and stick call throughout the model, including the sweeps and loft, to make sure everything binds to the body joint. I'm defining the root body joint at the origin facing along z and keeping all coordinates in model space so this explicit binding keeps orientation consistent.

Now I'm planning the remaining joint hierarchy -- prop (hinge), ailerons, elevator (hinge), rudder (hinge), wheels (hinge), head, and a scarf chain trailing from the neck using a catmull curve with three joints, swept with a tapering radius to give it a flowing tail shape.

Deciding to skip extra pennant streamers and extrude a flag as a static decoration instead, keeping the structural joints simpler. I'm also placing the pilot's torso and head within the cockpit -- a scaled brown jacket sphere around y1.85 and a head joint above it pointing upward.

Now I'm working out the head cap, goggle lenses, and strap torus placement against the wing's leading edge to confirm there's no overlap, then adding a dark coaming ellipsoid to suggest the cockpit opening against the fuselage top.

I'm running into ambiguity about how torus scaling interacts with rotation order, so I decide to sidestep it by building the rim as a flattened ellipse through a scaled torus geometry with no extra rotation, plus a dark circle beneath for the recessed cockpit interior.

Now I'm sketching the windscreen as a small tilted glass box with a frame, positioned just forward of the cabane at the right height and angle.

I'm adding a headrest fairing behind the pilot using a scaled sphere, plus a turtle deck bump further back for the fuselage profile. For the tail I'm extruding a wing-shaped stabilizer with defined span and chord near the rear, pairing it with a red elevator box at the trailing edge, and checking where the fuselage actually terminates to line things up correctly.

Now I'm positioning the elevator hinge and box geometry at the tail, then working out the fin's outline using a set of coordinates that sweep forward from the trailing edge, making sure the points stay in proper counterclockwise order for the shape to extrude cleanly.

I'm shaping the rudder similarly with its own outline and pivot joint, then adding whimsical paint details -- a heart-shaped rudder design with cream and red stripes computed from vertical position, and a red fin color scheme.

Now I'm working out the tail skid geometry, realizing the proposed mount points make the tail sit too high; I need to lower the fuselage's tail centerline to get a more realistic three-point stance close to the ground.

I'm adjusting the fuselage loft station heights from nose to tail, setting the tail skid as a tapered rod with a small shoe sphere at its tip, and confirming the cabane strut attaches at the fuselage top.

Now I'm positioning the cabane struts as two pairs of angled rods connecting the fuselage top to the upper wing at specific chord points, and checking that the fuselage width tapers correctly match where the lower wing root intersects the belly.

Adjusting strut positions to x=±3.0 so both wing outlines stay within chord bounds. For the wires, I'll keep it simple by adding crossing wire bracing in the vertical plane at each strut location rather than full lateral complexity.

For the roundel decal, I'm building an SVG texture with concentric circles in dark navy, yellow, red, and cream, topped with a small teal star shape for the national marking detail.

I'm also planning a fuselage name decal, a "SKYLARK" text graphic in bold sans-serif cream lettering with an ink outline, sized to fit on the fuselage side.

Now I'm working out placement of the decal and paint details: positioning the name on the forward red fuselage, adding a cream belly countershade and a cream cheat-line stripe near the tail, and mirroring the decal direction for the opposite side.

I'm also setting up the propeller blades as extruded shapes with outlines running from the hub to the tip, plus a thickness bevel, and defining the wheel joints and the tire geometry as a dark torus with specified tube and major radii.

Now I'm working out the hub (cream cylinder with a red cone cap), the landing gear struts as V-shaped cream rods connecting the body to the axle points, and a rigid dark axle rod running through the wheels so they can spin freely on it.

I'm deciding what extra details to add for character—thinking through small whimsical touches like wingtip nav lights (red/teal glowing spheres), skipping things like mascots or ribbons, and considering exhaust pipes for the final part count, aiming for roughly 120 parts total.

Placing twin exhaust pipes along the cowl sides with slightly curved paths, then adding small hemisphere engine bumps to simulate cylinder detail on the cowling.

Now I'm pruning down the imports to only what's actually used, settling on frame and catmull helpers plus paint and countershade for the color work, trimming unused pieces like glow or rng to keep the build clean.

Setting up builder and joint structure...

Adding the rudder and head joints, then starting on the scarf chain with a catmull curve path trailing from the head.

Still positioning head gear...

I'm giving the goggles googly eyes with white lenses and dark pupils for a whimsical touch, adding a small pink nose sphere, brown mustache spheres flattened and positioned under the nose, and considering pink cheek accents.

Now I'm building the torso as a scaled brown jacket sphere with capsule arms running from shoulders to skin-toned hand spheres, plus a small control stick rod, then moving on to fuselage cockpit trim and hull paint shading.

Still writing hull and wing paint logic...

Baked fabric cel colors should mix fine with normally-lit flat colors elsewhere. I'm defining a simple octagonal outline for the wing profile with corners cut at a fixed smoothing radius, then extruding it into the wing shape.

Still writing extrusion params...

I'm deciding to skip ailerons on the lower wings since the hinge geometry would look off, and instead focus on placing the aileron box on the upper wing trailing edge, checking that it fits within the wingspan without overlapping the tip.

I'm also sketching out small details like hinge nubs, wingtip navigation light spheres in red and green following aviation convention, and considering a pitot tube rod near the nose.

I'm thinking about adding a playful bunting string of small triangular flags sagging between the upper wing struts, using curved points to create a natural drooping line, though I need to check it doesn't clash with the cabane struts or cowl.

Checking clearances near the cabane struts and propeller top, the rope stays a safe 15cm away from everything. For the flags, I'm deciding to model them as flat extruded triangles attached along the rope, using a small triangular outline shape to keep them lightweight.

I'm defining the rope as a sagging polyline between two points, using a parabolic droop formula for the y-coordinate so it curves naturally downward in the middle, then sweeping a thin tube along that path for the actual rope geometry. Thirteen small triangular flags get placed at points along the rope, cycling through alternating colors.

I'm skipping extra wheel details for now, but adding a simple front axle fairing and a yellow prop spinner with a brass hub disk. Now I'm assembling everything into the final file, watching variable naming carefully in the loops and color arrays, and renaming unused paint callback parameters with underscores to avoid lint issues.

For the rudder paint, I'm computing horizontal stripe bands based on vertical position, alternating cream and red, double-checking the modulo math handles negative indices correctly so the banding stays consistent. Then I'm defining the tail skid as a swept path tapering down toward the ground, with a flattened sphere as the skid shoe scaled so its bottom just touches the ground plane.

Now I'm setting up the fuselage body as a lofted shape across elliptical station profiles with rounded tail caps, and planning a decal placement for the aircraft's name text on the fuselage surface using an SVG-rendered label. I'm also sketching out the metadata export (name, description, style, commit hash) before writing the final TypeScript code with proper typing and import paths.

Now I'm working out the cowl ring vents using oriented boxes following the surface normal, positioning a frame of items around the cowl radius near the cockpit, and verifying ground clearance between the wheels and skid stays non-negative. I'm also defining the propeller blade paint function, alternating between yellow and wood tones based on vertical position along the blade.
